concerns.issue: Gastritis is numbered C3, the same as Peptic Ulcer Disease on page 72; later sections (Cirrhosis C4 through Appendicitis C9) leave the chapter with 10 topics but only 9 numbers.
GERD management table: the first row label reads 'Antacids Proton Pump Inhibitors' with '(PPIs)' on the next row, so the antacid and PPI row labels run together.

Metoclopramide (GI stimulant) is given the same purpose as H2 blockers ('Reduce gastric acid production; useful in mild to moderate cases'), which looks copied from the row above; metoclopramide is a prokinetic, not an acid-reducing drug.
Esophageal pH monitoring lists normal as pH > 5 and abnormal as pH < 5; the usual reflux threshold is pH < 4, so this cutoff should be checked.

Normal serum amylase is given as 100-300 units/L and lipase is said to rise within 2 hours; both differ from commonly used references (amylase roughly 30-110 U/L; lipase rises about 4-8 hours after onset) and should be checked.

Avoiding morphine because of sphincter of Oddi spasm is older teaching that is no longer well supported. It also contradicts page 89, which says morphine is safe for acute abdominal pain, while pages 82 and 87 favor meperidine/Demerol.

The Remember box about Turner's sign and Cullen's sign is on a Cirrhosis page; these signs are listed as pancreatitis findings on page 69, so the box looks misplaced. Page 69 also calls it 'Grey Turner sign' while page 79 calls it 'Turner's sign'.
Typo: 'Ca ions bids to citrate' should read 'binds'.
Typo in the History box: 'fa-ttyy foods' should be 'fatty foods'.

'Medical dissolution is rare for nonobese patients with small cholesterol stones and a functional gallbladder' reads backwards; dissolution therapy is usually reserved for exactly those patients. The lab table also has the typo 'obststruction'.
Causes box lists 'meperidine, methylpredsisolone' under associated conditions for appendicitis without explanation; 'methylpredsisolone' is misspelled (methylprednisolone).
The Remember box on colostomy stoma assessment is in the Appendicitis section, but appendectomy does not normally create a colostomy, so it looks misplaced.
The diverticular disease causes text on page 87 repeats the Causes text on page 86 almost word for word.
In-text citation 'Bosch, Gracia-Sancho, & Abrades, 2020' does not match the reference list spelling 'Abraldes' (page 90).
In-text citation 'Barnes et al., 2022' does not match the reference list, which gives Barnes et al. (2020) (page 90).

The reference list has the same Chouairi et al. article twice (2021 advance online and 2022 print). That article is about gallstone pancreatitis cholecystectomy disparities but is cited for general pancreatitis (page 69) and cholecystitis (page 81) background.

Routine NG tube to suction and TPN 'within 3 days if needed' reflect older practice; current acute pancreatitis guidance favors early oral/enteral feeding, with NG suction for ileus or persistent vomiting and parenteral nutrition only if enteral feeding fails. Peritoneal lavage is also rarely used now. No questions were built on these points.
Sandostatin (octreotide) drip is listed for gastritis bleeding; octreotide is mainly used for variceal bleeding, so its place here should be checked. No questions were built on it.

Demerol (meperidine) is called the preferred analgesic for cholecystitis (also page 87 for diverticulitis); meperidine is now generally discouraged because of its neurotoxic metabolite. No questions were built on this.

5-ASA (mesalamine) is called first-line for Crohn disease; current guidelines find limited benefit of mesalamine in Crohn disease (it is first-line for ulcerative colitis). Questions avoid the 'first-line' claim.

In the Medical Management box, outpatient criteria and 'Initial treatment' are given without a source for the 48-hour/72-hour surgical timing; the open cholecystectomy 'within 72 hours' window should be checked.

The gastritis 'Pharmacologic Highlights' table (PPI, vasopressor, antibiotics, antacids, bismuth, vitamin B12) is printed on page 78, which falls in the Cirrhosis section's page range, so gastritis questions cannot link to it; the table may belong on page 77.
Urine output < 1 mL/kg/hr is given as the hypoperfusion signal; the threshold commonly used is < 0.5 mL/kg/hr, so this number should be checked. No v3 questions use it.
The Cirrhosis - Assessment History box is cut off at the bottom of the panel (text after 'Bleeding: Easy bruising, nosebleeds, bleeding gums' is clipped).

Nursing Care says 'Avoid strain: no heavy lifting, coughing'; advising clients to avoid coughing is unusual and may need rewording (e.g., splint when coughing). No v3 questions use the coughing advice.

"Cystic fibrosis is the leading cause in children" overstates current data; pediatric acute pancreatitis is most often biliary, drug-related, traumatic, systemic or idiopathic, while CFTR and other genetic causes lead in recurrent/chronic disease. A v3 item built on this was rewritten.

H. pylori serum IgG antibody testing is listed as an H. pylori test (also p76). Current guidelines advise against serology because it cannot tell active from past infection; urea breath, stool antigen or biopsy-based tests are preferred. Triple therapy with clarithromycin is also no longer the preferred first-line regimen in many regions.
"Malnutrition, protein deficiency" is listed as a cause of cirrhosis; this is not a recognized independent cause by current standards and should be checked.

Albumin is given as an example of IV fluid resuscitation alongside lactated Ringer's; current guidance favors goal-directed crystalloid (LR) and does not support routine albumin. Dopamine as the vasopressor is also older practice (norepinephrine is usually preferred).
Vasopressin infusion to stop gastritis bleeding (also p78 table) is older practice; current management relies on PPIs, endoscopic therapy and transfusion. Items only test its purpose.
